# The Weight of Unfinished Things

I'm thinking about the kitchen drawer at my mother's house, the one that holds everything nobody knows what to do with. Rubber bands from vegetables that came that way. A single AAA battery. Three pens that might work if you scribbled with them long enough. A takeout menu from a Thai place that closed five years ago. Post-it notes in colors that don't exist anymore. This drawer exists in almost every home, I think. It's a drawer of potential and procrastination, of things deemed too useful to throw away but not useful enough to have an assigned place.

I wonder if our minds are like that. If we all have mental drawers full of half-formed thoughts and conversations we never had and worries we set down but never quite resolved. Things we keep meaning to organize. Things we keep meaning to address.

There's a book on my nightstand I've been reading for eighteen months. Not because it's bad, but because I keep forgetting I'm reading it. I'll pick it up, read fifteen pages, remember there's laundry downstairs, and when I come back to it weeks later, I have to reread those fifteen pages because they've evaporated. This has happened four times now. I know it's a good book. I like the author's sentences. They have weight to them. But somewhere between my eyes and my memory, the story isn't sticking. Maybe I'm not ready for it. Maybe I'm too tired. Maybe I'm just not the kind of person who finishes books anymore, and I should accept that instead of this recurring cycle of hope and disappointment.

This thought leads me to other unfinished things: emails I've drafted but not sent, conversations I've rehearsed but chickened out on, New Year's resolutions from three years ago that I haven't deleted from my phone because deleting them feels like admitting defeat. There's a sweater I started knitting in 2019. It's beautiful yarn, a color like ocean water, and I got about halfway done before I realized I'd made some catastrophic mistake in the pattern and would have to unravel half my work to fix it. I haven't touched it since. Sometimes I see it in the closet and feel a small shame, as if the sweater is disappointed in me.

Do unfinished things accumulate in us like sediment? Do they build up and change us?

I read somewhere that our brains are wired to remember incomplete tasks better than completed ones. There's an actual term for this—the Zeigarnik Effect—named after a Soviet psychologist who noticed that waiters had better recall of unpaid orders than paid ones. Once something is done, our mind releases it. But unfinished business? It loops. It demands attention. It's like a song stuck in your head, except instead of a melody it's the nagging sense that you haven't quite lived up to what you meant to do.

Maybe this is why I'm thinking about it at eleven PM on a Tuesday, unable to sleep.

I have a friend who keeps a list of every book she wants to read. The list is now over three hundred items long. I asked her once if it stressed her out, having such an enormous list. She said sometimes, but mostly it made her feel like her life was full of possibility. I understand that feeling. It's the opposite of being trapped. It's abundant. But I wonder if there's a point where possibility becomes paralyzing. When you have too many unfinished things, can you ever actually be free?

Or maybe the opposite is true. Maybe finishing everything is the real trap—ending all the stories, resolving all the ambiguity, turning potential into concrete fact. Maybe it's actually beautiful to live with some amount of unfinishedness, like how a sketch can be more dynamic than a finished painting, how silence between notes is part of what makes music.

I have a habit of starting projects with enormous enthusiasm. I have a sewing machine I used for approximately three weeks. A bread starter named Gerald that I kept forgetting to feed until it died. A philosophy course I was auditing that required way more focus than I thought. A journal I started where I wrote exactly six entries and then stopped. Sometimes I see these abandoned things and feel like they're evidence of my fundamental flakiness, proof that I can't commit to anything. But maybe they're also evidence of my curiosity, my willingness to try. Maybe starting things is its own kind of completion.

The unfinished things in my life aren't always failures. Some of them are relationships in their natural state of becoming—friendships that are still forming, with new layers discovered each time we talk. Some are projects that are deliberately open-ended because closure would diminish them. Some are questions I'm not ready to answer yet, and that's okay. That's actually probably wise. Not every question needs an answer immediately. Some things need to sit in that kitchen drawer for a while, next to the mysterious batteries and expired menus, until we figure out what to do with them.

I think what I'm trying to say is that I've been treating incompleteness like a character flaw when maybe it's just a character trait. Maybe it's part of being human. We're all unfinished. We're all works in progress. The book will eventually be read or it won't, and either way, the book will be fine. The sweater will be finished or it will become something else—a scarf, a headband, a memory. The emails I'm afraid to send will either be sent or they won't, and the universe will keep turning.

The kitchen drawer will remain full. And that's not really a problem at all—it's just a drawer in a house where someone lives, full of the small accumulated moments of a life in progress. And that life is still being written. That's the whole point.
